trails.name: The Freedom Trail
trails.summary: Two and a half miles of red brick through sixteen Revolutionary sites, from Boston Common to the Bunker Hill Monument. The line is painted and inlaid into the pavement, so you cannot get lost, and you can join or leave it anywhere.

stops.name: Boston Common
stops.desc: Where the trail starts, and America's oldest public park. Militia drilled here, cows grazed here until 1830, and the redcoats camped here before Lexington.

stops.name: Massachusetts State House
stops.desc: The gold dome above the Common, finished 1798 on John Hancock's cow pasture. The dome was wood, then copper rolled by Paul Revere, and it is gold leaf now.
stops.yiki: Stand across the street and look straight up. In the Second World War they painted the dome grey so it would not shine for bombers off the coast. It is gold again now, and on a clear morning you have to squint.

stops.name: Park Street Church
stops.desc: The corner was once the town granary, then a powder store in 1812, which is why locals called it Brimstone Corner. America Is My Country was first sung here in 1831.
stops.yiki: Pick out the tall white steeple from a few streets away. For years it was the first thing a traveler saw riding into Boston, so you can arrive at it the way they did.

stops.name: Granary Burying Ground
stops.desc: Samuel Adams, John Hancock, Paul Revere and the five who died in the Boston Massacre are all in this one small yard. The headstones were rearranged for lawnmowers, so the stones and the graves no longer match.
stops.yiki: Find the tall obelisk in the centre. It marks Benjamin Franklin's mother and father, though Franklin himself lies in Philadelphia. Read a few of the winged skulls while you are here, the carving softens as the century turns.

stops.name: King's Chapel
stops.desc: The first Anglican church in Puritan Boston, deeply unwelcome, so it was built around the old wooden one and the timber was thrown out the windows. The bell is Revere's largest.
stops.yiki: Notice the tower stops square and plain. The steeple it was drawn for was never built, the money ran out, and Bostonians rather grew to like it unfinished. Inside, the high box pews were rented by the family.

stops.name: Boston Latin School site
stops.desc: The first public school in America, 1635. Benjamin Franklin went here and did not graduate. His statue stands on the spot.
stops.yiki: Look down, not up. The schoolhouse is long gone, and the spot is a mosaic set into the pavement. Several signers of the Declaration learned their Latin here before Franklin did, and left better credentialed than he managed to.

stops.name: Old Corner Bookstore
stops.desc: The oldest commercial building downtown, 1718, and the publishing house that printed Hawthorne, Emerson, Longfellow and Stowe. It is a Chipotle now, which locals will tell you about at length.
stops.yiki: It was nearly a parking lot. A handful of Bostonians bought the building in nineteen sixty to stop the wreckers, and that one fight started the group that has since saved a good deal of what you will walk past today.

stops.name: Old South Meeting House
stops.desc: Five thousand colonists packed in here on 16 December 1773, could not get the tea sent back, and walked out to the harbour. The Tea Party started in this room.
stops.yiki: When the British held the town they tore out the pews and rode horses inside, to insult the very room where it had started. Stand in the middle and picture it packed to the walls, because on that December night it was.

stops.name: Old State House
stops.desc: The oldest surviving public building in Boston, 1713, with the lion and unicorn still on the gable. The Declaration of Independence was read from that balcony in 1776 and is read from it every Fourth of July.
stops.yiki: The lion and the unicorn are the crown's own animals, and in seventeen seventy six the crowd pulled the first pair down and burned them in the street. These are later copies, put back once the anger had cooled. A subway runs directly under the floor now.

stops.name: Boston Massacre Site
stops.desc: A ring of cobblestones in a traffic island. Five men died here on 5 March 1770, and John Adams defended the soldiers in court because he thought the trial mattered more than the verdict.
stops.yiki: Mind the traffic to reach it, then look back up at the balcony above you, because the two places are one story. The first of the five to fall was Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Wampanoag descent.

stops.name: Faneuil Hall
stops.desc: The meeting hall where the argument for revolution was made out loud, 1742, with the grasshopper weather vane still on top. Food stalls downstairs, the hall itself upstairs and free.

stops.name: Paul Revere House
stops.desc: The oldest house in downtown Boston, about 1680, and he owned it on the night of the ride. Small, dark, low ceilings, and the most convincing room on the whole trail.
stops.yiki: Duck your head, the doorways were built for smaller people. He raised a large family in these few rooms across two marriages, and the tightness of the place tells you more about the man than any label on the wall.

stops.name: Old North Church
stops.desc: One if by land, two if by sea. The two lanterns were hung in this steeple for about a minute on 18 April 1775, long enough to be seen across the water and not long enough to be caught.
stops.yiki: Revere did not hang the lanterns himself. That was Robert Newman, the sexton, who climbed the steeple and then slipped out a back window to get home unseen. Look up into the dark where he stood.

stops.name: Copp's Hill Burying Ground
stops.desc: The high ground the British used to shell Charlestown during Bunker Hill. Headstones here still carry musket damage from redcoats using them as targets.
stops.yiki: Walk to the far corner and look across the water. That rise is Charlestown and the monument you are heading for, so you can see the end of the walk from here. Many of Boston's free Black residents are buried in this ground.

stops.name: USS Constitution
stops.desc: Old Ironsides, launched 1797, still a commissioned Navy ship and the oldest warship afloat anywhere. Active duty sailors give the tours. Bring photo identification.

stops.name: Bunker Hill Monument
stops.desc: The end of the trail, and 294 steps with no lift. The battle was actually fought on Breed's Hill, the colonists lost, and it still convinced everyone the war was winnable.
stops.yiki: Two hundred and ninety four steps, and a small triumph at the top, since most people stop counting near two hundred. This is where they were told to hold their fire until they could see the whites of the enemy's eyes, because powder was too scarce to waste a shot.

trails.name: The National Mall
trails.summary: Two miles along one straight axis, from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial and round the Tidal Basin to Jefferson: eighteen stops, most of them free, and the only walk in the country where you can see the next monument from the one you are standing at. Distances are straight-line along the Mall's straight paths, marked as estimates, not routed.

stops.name: United States Capitol
stops.desc: The east end of the axis and the building everything else is measured from. The dome is cast iron painted to look like stone, and the Statue of Freedom on top faces east, away from the Mall.

stops.name: United States Botanic Garden
stops.desc: The oldest continually operating botanic garden in the country, in a conservatory at the foot of Capitol Hill. Free, warm, and the place to get out of the weather.

stops.name: National Museum of the American Indian
stops.desc: Curved limestone meant to read as wind-carved rock, the only museum on the Mall whose building refuses the axis. The cafe is the best on the Mall.

stops.name: National Air and Space Museum
stops.desc: The Wright Flyer, the Spirit of St. Louis and the Apollo 11 command module under one roof. Timed passes, free, and they go fast.

stops.name: National Gallery of Art
stops.desc: The West Building is the marble one, the East Building is the angles. Free, and the only Leonardo in the Americas is in the West.

stops.name: Hirshhorn Museum
stops.desc: The concrete drum on legs, and the sculpture garden sunk beside it. Modern and contemporary, free, and the building is the first exhibit.

stops.name: Smithsonian Castle
stops.desc: Red sandstone and towers, 1855, the Smithsonian's first building and its front door. Closed for renovation at the time of writing; the outside is the visit.

stops.name: National Museum of Natural History
stops.desc: The elephant in the rotunda, the Hope Diamond upstairs, and more visitors than any other museum on the Mall. Go early or go at four.

stops.name: National Museum of American History
stops.desc: The Star-Spangled Banner in a dark room, Dorothy's ruby slippers, and the flag that was the anthem. Free.

stops.name: National Museum of African American History and Culture
stops.desc: The bronze corona, three tiers widening as they rise, the newest museum on the Mall and the one that needs the most time. Timed passes, free.

stops.name: Washington Monument
stops.desc: The tallest stone structure in the world, and the colour changes a third of the way up where construction stopped for twenty-two years. Tickets for the top are timed and free.

stops.name: World War II Memorial
stops.desc: Fifty-six pillars around the pool, one per state and territory, between the Monument and the Reflecting Pool. The Freedom Wall carries 4,048 gold stars, one for every hundred dead.

stops.name: Vietnam Veterans Memorial
stops.desc: Two black granite arms sunk into the ground, 58,000 names in the order they died. Bring paper for a rubbing; the rangers have pencils.

stops.name: Lincoln Memorial
stops.desc: Thirty-six columns for the states at Lincoln's death, and the step where King stood is marked. Best at dawn and after dark, when it is lit and the crowds are gone.

stops.name: Korean War Veterans Memorial
stops.desc: Nineteen steel soldiers walking through juniper, and a black granite wall that reflects them into thirty-eight, for the parallel. Go at dusk.

stops.name: Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial
stops.desc: The Stone of Hope pulled forward out of the Mountain of Despair, on the Tidal Basin between Lincoln and Jefferson, on a line that was chosen on purpose.

stops.name: Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial
stops.desc: Four outdoor rooms, one per term, with waterfalls, along the Tidal Basin. The only presidential memorial you walk through rather than up to.

stops.name: Jefferson Memorial
stops.desc: The rotunda across the water from the Monument, on axis with the White House. The cherry trees around it are the ones people come in April for.
